measurement.happened:
This week in Taiwan was dominated by a severe stock market selloff, intense international diplomacy, and a wave of AI-fueled cultural excitement in Taipei. Let me walk through the themes.

THE STOCK MARKET CRASH. This is the single biggest story of the week. Bloomberg reported that Taiwan stocks plunged again to head for the worst week since 1991, and that Barclays identified forced retail selling as the driver of the rout. In response, the Taiwan stock exchange said it would ensure stable operation of capital markets, and the government enacted new short-selling curbs to support the market. Bloomberg also noted the currency paradox: the AI boom has left the New Taiwan Dollar behind, meaning the currency is not benefiting from the same tech-driven growth as the equities. The broader context is that Bloomberg asked whether Taiwan's "island of super rich" will last, suggesting the crash is hitting a market that had been propped up by a small number of wealthy investors and AI-related names. The forced retail selling angle is particularly telling: it suggests that when the big players pulled back, ordinary investors were trapped and sold in a panic, amplifying the drop. This is a liquidity and confidence crisis more than a fundamentals crisis, but the speed of the decline (worst since 1991) means the psychological damage could be significant. (Headlines: Bloomberg Nov 17, 19, 20, 21; Reuters Nov 19; Bloomberg Nov 16, 17.)

US-CHINA-TAIWAN DIPLOMACY AND THE APEC BACKDROP. The week was heavy with great-power maneuvering. Xi told the US it should do the "right thing" on Taiwan to avoid setbacks in relations, a clear signal that the Taiwan question is a bargaining chip in the broader US-China relationship. Bloomberg's takeaways from Trump's China trip listed AI, nuclear arms, and Taiwan as the three big topics, and CNBC noted that US-China trade, Taiwan, and tech tensions remain unresolved as Trump returned from Asia. Taiwan was reportedly in "close contact" with the US ahead of the US-China-Russia talks at APEC, and Bloomberg observed that Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time. The US also pressed a UN agency over Taiwan flight restrictions, with China hitting back, a smaller but pointed diplomatic friction. Bloomberg's piece on America's support for Taiwan looking "alarmingly fragile" captures the anxiety in Taipei: the US is negotiating with China, and Taiwan is not at the table. (Headlines: Reuters Nov 18, 19; Bloomberg Nov 16, 19; CNBC Nov 20; Reuters Nov 17.)

JAPAN-CHINA TAIWAN RIFT. A year after PM Takaichi's remarks on Taiwan sparked a rift with China, the two leaders shook hands at what appears to be a summit, and Takaichi said Japan's position on Taiwan has not changed. Reuters framed this as a year-long diplomatic wound that is being patched over but not healed. This matters for Taiwan because Japan is one of its closest allies, and any softening of Japan's stance would shift the regional balance. (Headlines: Reuters Nov 18, 19; Bloomberg Nov 18.)

RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT INCURSIONS. Taiwan reported two Russian military aircraft flying nearby, the second time in the same week. Japan and Taiwan jointly flagged these incursions ahead of Putin's arrival in China. This is a notable signal: Russia is testing the airspace around the Taiwan Strait, likely to see how the US, Japan, and Taiwan react while the great powers are in a delicate diplomatic moment at APEC. It is a low-cost way for Moscow to remind everyone it is still a player in the Western Pacific. (Headlines: Reuters Nov 18, 19.)

NVIDIA, AI, AND THE "JENSANITY" PHENOMENON. Taipei 101 displayed messages of support for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and the Financial Times described a virtual "Jensanity" rocking Taipei in support of the Nvidia chief. Bloomberg reported that Nvidia sought Taipei's help over an employee's chip-smuggling case, a reminder that the AI chip supply chain runs through Taiwan in ways that create both cooperation and friction. Delta Electronics said it looks to triple its India revenue in four to five years on the AI boom, showing the ripple effects of the AI wave through Taiwan's supply chain. This is a genuinely unusual cultural moment: a tech CEO becoming almost a national hero in a small island democracy, with the tallest building in the city projecting his name. (Headlines: CNN Nov 17; FT Nov 19; Bloomberg Nov 15; Reuters Nov 19.)

DIPLOMATIC ISOLATION AND FRIENDSHIPS STRAINED. Papua New Guinea's prime minister told Xi it "wasn't easy" to close Taiwan's representative office, a small but symbolic loss in the diaspora network. South Africa demanded Taiwan move its Pretoria office, and Taiwan reportedly "ignored" the demand. Taiwan warned Canada's PM Mark Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks, a pointed message to a G7 leader. The foreign minister made a second US trip in two months, underscoring how actively Taipei is working to maintain its relationships. (Headlines: Reuters Nov 17; Bloomberg Nov 17; AP Nov 21; Reuters Nov 17.)

CHINA-LINKED DIGITAL INFLUENCE. In an exclusive, Reuters reported that Taiwan told Meta that thousands of China-linked accounts are seeking to influence elections. This is a quiet but important story: it suggests Beijing is running a sustained, low-level information operation aimed at Taiwan's electoral process, and that Taipei is trying to get the social media platform to act. (Headline: Reuters Nov 20.)

EU STEEL TARIFFS. The EU set tariffs on steel from several countries including Taiwan, a trade friction point that is relatively minor compared to the other stories but adds to the sense that Taiwan is being squeezed from multiple directions in global trade. (Headline: Reuters Nov 16.)

CLIMATE-RESILIENT AGRICULTURE. TV5Monde reported on the return of an ancestral cereal in Taiwan that is resistant to climate change, a small but hopeful story about food security and heritage agriculture adapting to a warming world. (Headline: TV5Monde Nov 15.)

Almost certain: the short-selling curbs and exchange interventions will dominate the first few trading days of next week as investors try to gauge whether the selling has bottomed. The government will likely issue further statements about market stability, and the central bank may be asked to comment on the New Taiwan Dollar's weakness. Probable: if the forced retail selling identified by Barclays continues, we could see another 2-3 percent drop early in the week before a technical bounce. The super-rich concentration issue will keep generating commentary. Possible: the government might announce a small stimulus or liquidity injection if the market does not stabilize by Wednesday. Unlikely: a full-blown circuit-breaker event or a change in interest rates within this single week.

US-CHINA-TAIWAN DIPLOMACY. Almost certain: the fallout from the APEC summit and Trump's China trip will continue to generate headlines. Beijing will likely press the "right thing" rhetoric in official statements, and Washington will respond with its own framing. Probable: Taiwan's foreign minister or a senior official will make another public statement about the US-Taiwan relationship, possibly in response to a specific US policy signal. The UN flight-restrictions dispute will see at least one more round of diplomatic notes. Possible: a small US congressional delegation or a senior State Department official will visit Taipei or hold a virtual call. Unlikely: a major new US arms deal announcement or a formal change in the US position on Taiwan within seven days.

JAPAN-CHINA AND RUSSIAN ACTIVITY. Probable: Japan and Taiwan will continue to coordinate on the Russian aircraft incursions, possibly issuing a joint statement or a bilateral complaint. Russia may fly another reconnaissance pass to test the waters, especially if the APEC diplomacy is still generating headlines. Possible: China will make a pointed remark about Russia's Pacific activity to signal its own regional reach. Unlikely: a direct confrontation or a formal incident between Russia and either Japan or Taiwan.

NVIDIA / AI / TECH. Almost certain: the "Jensanity" cultural moment will continue to generate social media buzz and local media coverage, especially if Nvidia or Jensen Huang makes any public statement. Probable: the chip-smuggling case involving a Nvidia employee will see at least one more development, possibly a court hearing or a statement from the prosecution. The Delta Electronics India expansion story will be picked up by business media as a sign of the AI supply chain's geographic spread. Possible: a new AI-related policy announcement from the government, perhaps tied to the stock market recovery narrative. Unlikely: a major new AI breakthrough or a significant Nvidia product announcement specifically targeting the Taiwan market.

DIGITAL INFLUENCE AND ELECTIONS. Probable: Meta will respond to the Reuters exclusive with a statement, possibly confirming or denying the scale of the China-linked accounts. The opposition parties in Taiwan will likely use the story to press the ruling party on its digital defense strategy. Possible: a small parliamentary or committee hearing on foreign influence in digital spaces. Unlikely: a formal investigation or a new law on foreign digital influence within this one week.

DIPLOMATIC OFFICES AND ALLIANCES. Possible: South Africa may follow up on its demand about the Pretoria office, and Taiwan's response (or non-response) will be noted. The Papua New Guinea story will fade from headlines but remain a talking point in diplomatic circles. Probable: Taiwan will issue a general statement about maintaining its global friendships. Unlikely: a new country will close or open a Taiwan representative office within this week.

AGRICULTURE AND CLIMATE. Possible: the ancestral cereal story will get a follow-up in agricultural or climate media, but it is unlikely to be a major political event. Unlikely: any new climate policy announcement tied to this specific crop.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES (low probability but not zero): A sudden US-China trade deal announcement that specifically mentions Taiwan's semiconductor role, which would send the stock market sharply higher. A minor earthquake in the Taiwan Strait region that briefly disrupts trading and adds to the anxiety. A public spat between Taiwan and the EU over the steel tariffs escalating into a broader trade complaint. A surprise visit by a US military aircraft or carrier group to the waters near Taiwan, timed to coincide with the Russian incursions.

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON: A major political crisis such as a cabinet resignation or a snap election announcement. A direct military clash between Taiwan and China, or between Taiwan and Russia. A full-scale stock market crash with a 10-plus percent single-day drop. A new trade war between Taiwan and the US. A significant change in the US dollar or New Taiwan Dollar exchange rate beyond normal weekly fluctuation. A major natural disaster such as a typhoon or earthquake. A new pandemic or health emergency. A formal declaration of independence or a major shift in the one-China policy framework.
emoji_reasons: The stock market's worst week since 1991, the short-selling ban, and the forced retail selling panic are the single most consequential domestic event of the week.

The APEC summit, Xi-Trump-Takaichi diplomacy, Russian aircraft incursions, the UN flight-restrictions dispute, and the Papua New Guinea and South Africa office issues make international relations the dominant backdrop.

The Taipei 101 'Jensanity' display, the Nvidia chip-smuggling case, Delta Electronics' AI-driven India expansion, and the broader AI boom context make artificial intelligence the defining cultural and economic story.

delta.motion:
The most dramatic shift between the two photographs is the stock market. One week it jumped more than a thousand points on a Wall Street rally; the next it posted its worst week since 1991, driven by forced retail selling and a government scramble to curb short-selling. The mood flipped from bullish to panicked in a single five-day stretch, and the narrative changed from 'exports surging on AI demand' to 'will the island of super-rich last?' The currency, meanwhile, quietly fell behind, underscoring that the AI boom was not evenly shared.

The Jensen Huang story did not vanish but changed shape. In the first photograph it was a scandal: affairs, a spy-thriller subplot with a Chinese woman and a Hong Kong passport, an FBI probe, a damaged 'hometown hero' image, and a Micron union calling its bonus talks a defeat. By the second photograph the scandal had softened into something almost celebratory — Taipei 101 projecting messages of support, the Financial Times coining 'Jensanity' — while the operational friction sharpened: Nvidia asking Taipei's help with a chip-smuggling case. The Micron union and the FBI investigation details faded from the headlines. The story moved from personal drama to institutional cooperation.

China-Taiwan tension grew in volume but shifted in form. The first photograph featured Xi's reunification speech, unannounced Pacific drills, a G7 joint statement, and a tourist-squabble. The second photograph shows the same tension reframed through US-China diplomacy: Xi telling the US to do the 'right thing' on Taiwan, Trump and Xi meeting for a third time with Taiwan reportedly taking a backseat, and the US pressing a UN agency over flight restrictions while China hits back. The military posturing that was visible in week one became, in week two, a diplomatic and bargaining-chip story. A new actor appeared: Russia, with two aircraft incursions in a single week, testing the airspace while the great powers were in a delicate APEC moment. That thread was absent from the first photograph entirely.

Diplomatic activity broadened and, in some cases, narrowed. The first photograph showed Germany visiting, US federal employees entering Taiwan offices, and APEC 'equal basis' language. The second photograph shows Japan and China shaking hands a year after the Takaichi rift, Papua New Guinea closing Taiwan's representative office, South Africa demanding Taiwan move its Pretoria office, and Taiwan warning Canada that deeper China ties carry risks. The net effect is a sense of diplomatic erosion at the margins even as the high-level US-China channel dominates the center.

A new thread appeared that had no counterpart in the first photograph: China-linked digital influence. Reuters reported that Taiwan told Meta that thousands of Beijing-linked accounts are trying to shape elections. This is a quieter, more structural form of the transnational-repression pressure that showed up in week one as violent attacks on critics. The physical intimidation faded; the digital operation emerged.

Smaller threads appeared and vanished. The sovereign-wealth-fund draft, the Foxconn supply-chain warning, and the specific FBI investigation details from week one are absent from week two. In their place: EU steel tariffs on Taiwan, Delta Electronics tripling its India revenue on the AI boom, and a TV5Monde piece on a climate-resilient ancestral cereal. The Micron union, the G7 foreign-ministers statement, and the Chinese-woman-spy subplot all shrank out of the headlines.

In speed: the market crash was the fastest-moving story, reversing a week of gains in a single trading week. The diplomatic realignment around APEC and the Trump-Xi meetings developed over the full week. The Russian incursions and the Japan-China handshake were discrete events landing mid-week. The Nvidia 'Jensanity' and the Meta/China-accounts stories were slower-burn reveals that accumulated over several days.
delta.wind:
On the Nvidia/Jensen Huang front, the expectation was that the scandal would keep generating headlines, the FBI investigation would be followed up, the Micron union would file a grievance, and the 'hometown hero' narrative would be questioned. What actually happened was a partial inversion: the scandal softened into a cultural celebration ('Jensanity,' Taipei 101 displays), while the operational friction (chip smuggling) became the harder story. The Micron union and the FBI probe details largely faded. The expectation was directionally right that the story would continue, but wrong about its emotional register — it healed into pride rather than souring into loss.

On China-Taiwan military and diplomatic posturing, the expectation was that Beijing would keep referencing the Pacific drills, that another G7 or NATO-adjacent body would issue language about stability, and that a small unannounced exercise or strait transit might occur. What happened was broader and more consequential: the tension was absorbed into the US-China relationship at the highest level (Trump-Xi meetings, Xi telling the US to do the 'right thing'), and a new actor (Russia) tested the airspace twice. The G7-language expectation was partly met through the APEC backdrop but in a form that actually sidelined Taiwan rather than elevating it. The 'small unannounced exercise' expectation was close but the actor was Russia, not China. The 'no full-scale crisis' expectation was correct.

On diplomatic and trade activity, the expectation was that APEC follow-up would produce headlines about 'equal basis' and written guarantees, that the US federal-employee scheme would be detailed, and that the German visit might yield a small agreement. What happened was that APEC became the stage for a Trump-Xi meeting where Taiwan was reportedly in the background, the US federal-employee scheme faded from the headlines, and the German thread was replaced by the Japan-China handshake. The 'no major trade deal or sharp dispute' expectation was mostly right, though the EU steel tariff was a minor new friction point that was not anticipated.

On economy and markets, the expectation was that strong exports and the stock rally would set a positive tone, the sovereign-wealth-fund draft would be debated in the Legislative Yuan, and Foxconn or TSMC might issue a supply-chain update. Reality was the opposite on the market: the worst week since 1991, forced retail selling, new short-selling curbs. The sovereign-wealth-fund discussion did not surface in the headlines. The Foxconn thread was replaced by Delta Electronics' India expansion. The 'no sudden tariff shock' expectation was broadly correct, with the minor EU steel tariff as a small exception. This is the biggest miss in the forecast: the model assumed continuity from a rally, and the market delivered a sharp reversal.

On transnational repression, the expectation was a parliamentary question or a small demonstration following the violent attacks, and no major new arrest. What happened was a shift from physical to digital: the Meta/China-linked-accounts story. The 'no major new case' expectation was correct, but the form of the pressure changed.

Among the listed surprises, the 'brief but sharp drop in the TAIWAN SE index' happened but was far from brief — it was the defining story of the week. The 'Chinese naval vessel entering the 12-nautical-mile zone' was close in spirit but the actor was Russia with aircraft, not a Chinese ship. The 'surprise US State Department statement on APEC language' did not materialize in that form; instead, the US was negotiating with China directly. The 'second Micron or TSMC labor walkout' did not appear.

Things that were not expected at all: the Russian aircraft incursions, the Japan-China handshake, the 'Jensanity' cultural phenomenon, the Meta/China-accounts exclusive, the Papua New Guinea and South Africa diplomatic losses, the Delta Electronics India expansion, and the climate-resilient cereal story. The forecast was anchored too tightly to the specific threads of the first photograph and underweighted the possibility that the market would reverse, that Russia would insert itself, and that the Nvidia story would heal rather than deepen.

What this says about the way expectations have been wrong for this country: the forecasting model tends to project forward the specific stories of the prior week and assume their emotional register will hold. In Taiwan's case, the stories are more volatile and more subject to sudden reframing than the model captures. A scandal can become a celebration in a week. A rally can become a crash. A bilateral tension can be absorbed into a trilateral negotiation. A physical threat can become a digital one. The model needs to weight 'reframing' and 'actor substitution' more heavily for this country than for others where the storylines are more linear.
delta.driver: The force pushing Taiwan from the first photograph to the second is the collision between an AI-driven market concentrated in a small number of wealthy holders and a great-power diplomatic moment in which Taiwan is not at the table. The AI boom built the rally, the cultural phenomenon around Jensen Huang, and the export strength, but it also created the vulnerability: when the big players pulled back, forced retail selling turned a correction into the worst week since 1991. Simultaneously, the US and China were renegotiating their relationship at the highest level — Trump and Xi meeting for a third time, Xi telling Washington to do the 'right thing' on Taiwan — and in that negotiation Taiwan was a topic, not a participant. Russia tested the airspace to remind everyone it is still a player. Japan and China patched a year-old rift. Small Pacific and African partners quietly closed or repositioned Taiwan offices. The net effect is a country whose economic identity is tied to a single technological wave while its geopolitical position is being redrawn by powers that treat it as a bargaining chip, a test case, or a footnote in a larger deal. The motion from photograph one to photograph two is the sound of that collision: the market cracking, the diplomacy tightening, and the cultural pride around a tech CEO standing as a small bright spot in a week of structural pressure.

crystal.eli5:
Taiwan's stock market just had its worst week since 1991. That sounds scary, but here is the thing: the companies that make the chips for AI and smartphones are still doing great, and the government is already trying to fix the problem by making it harder for traders to bet against the market. So next week, the main story will be whether the market starts to feel better. It probably will, a little, but it will be a nervous, shaky kind of recovery, not a big triumphant one. Think of it like a kid who scraped their knee badly and is now walking around with a bandage, trying to act normal but still wincing.

At the same time, the big countries — the US and China — just had a big meeting in Asia, and Taiwan was not really at the table. China's leader told the US to do the 'right thing' about Taiwan, which is a polite way of saying 'don't forget we are watching.' So next week, everyone will be reading and re-reading what was said at that meeting, and Taiwan will be trying to make sure its friends still remember it exists. It is a bit like being the kid in the family who is not invited to the parents' dinner but still has to eat dinner at home.

There is also the fun one: everyone in Taipei was going crazy about Jensen Huang, the boss of Nvidia, the company that makes the chips for AI. The tallest building in the city put his name on the lights. It was a really cool, proud moment for the island. But that kind of excitement does not last forever. Next week, the lights will probably come down, and the story will shift to a smaller, more boring thing: a case where someone at Nvidia allegedly smuggled chips out of the country. The AI boom is still going, and Taiwan is still at the center of it, but the party is winding down and the paperwork is starting.
